issues.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition requires compensation to be assessed for all interests in the acquired land and then apportioned among the persons interested, regardless of whether the holder of the superior interest objected to the award.
material_facts: The acquisition covered land in which one person held superior ownership rights and another held subordinate land rights and owned the building.
The holder of the superior rights did not object to the Land Acquisition Officer’s award.
The subordinate rights holder objected to the amount of compensation.
issues.conclusion: The Land Acquisition Officer had to assess compensation for the acquired unit and apportion it among all persons interested; the superior rights holder’s failure to object did not alter that duty, and the subordinate rights holder was entitled to apportionment in respect of the land.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3(a) and 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, land is acquired as a unit, the Collector must determine the compensation for the land and apportion it among persons known or believed to be interested, and compulsory acquisition extinguishes outstanding interests not vested in the Government. A subordinate holder with an interest in the land is entitled to apportionment even if the holder of superior rights does not object.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns compensation for compulsorily acquired land with multiple interests, including a subordinate holder’s interest in the land, the compensation is assessed for the unit and apportioned among those interested even if the superior holder did not object.

issues.legal_issue: Land and a building acquired together must be valued as one composite property rather than by separately valuing the land and the building at its break-up value.
material_facts: The acquired unit consisted of land and a building used for business purposes.
The Land Acquisition Officer valued the land and the building separately, using a break-up value for the building.
The courts below treated the land and building as a composite property.
issues.conclusion: The separate valuation method was unwarranted; the entire unit had to be valued together, taking account of its advantages and potentialities.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, compensation is based on market value at the relevant date. For land with a building, the land and building constitute one unit and must be valued together, with their advantages and potentialities considered.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns compulsorily acquired land and a building that together constitute one property, the property is valued as a composite unit.

issues.legal_issue: Capitalisation of actual or reasonably obtainable rental income is an appropriate method for valuing land with buildings when reliable comparable sales are difficult to obtain.
material_facts: The acquired unit included a building used for business purposes and produced rental income.
Reliable evidence of sales of similar land with buildings close to the notification date was difficult to obtain.
Evidence of the rental income from the property was available.
issues.conclusion: Capitalisation of the net rental income was an appropriate method for determining the value of the acquired unit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act requires determination of market value at the relevant date. Raja Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. The Revenue Divisional Officer, Vizagapatnam explains that prices for similar property can guide market value; where reliable comparable sales of land with buildings are difficult to obtain, capitalisation of the return actually received or reasonably obtainable is a method generally used, especially for business property.

issues.definition: When comparable sales are difficult to obtain for compulsorily acquired land with a building and rental evidence is available, rental-income capitalisation is an appropriate valuation method.

issues.legal_issue: A multiple based on the return from gilt-edged securities is not a universal rule for capitalising rental income, but a lower court’s chosen multiple may be upheld when its basis is appropriate and no specific ground for rejecting it is shown.
material_facts: The trial court capitalised the net annual rental using a multiple informed by the return from gilt-edged securities.
The High Court reduced the multiple while retaining that valuation approach.
The State gave no ground for rejecting the lower courts’ basis or rate of capitalisation, and did not challenge the same multiple used in other acquisitions under the same notification.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to treat the gilt-edged securities return as a universally applicable rule, but found no ground to disturb the lower courts’ chosen basis and rate of capitalisation in this case.
issues.legal_principle: The market value of land with buildings may be determined by capitalising actual or reasonably obtainable returns, but no general rule makes a multiple approximately equal to the return on gilt-edged securities adequate in every case. The appropriateness of the multiple depends on the circumstances and the evidence; the Court relied on the absence of a specific ground for rejecting the lower courts’ assessment.
